utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon, after a break of one week, to everyone in and around this courtroom. I'd like to start first with one remaining procedural issue, that is, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that we have a number of exhibits where the OTP, and I'm asking specific attention to the parties for the fact that these are exhibits that were tendered under seal. I'm talking about the numbers P200 to P203, that the OTP would have gotten back to the Defence on Friday, the 15th of October, and that the Defence would then take a position on admission by today. I'm not inviting you to express yourselves on the contents of these exhibits, but has the Defence taken a position? Has the Defence received information from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Your Honour, that was a matter I was going to raise today, and fortunately, Your Honour has. In fact, we have not received that information, that selection from the Prosecution at this stage. I think that was meant to be by the 15th, as Your Honour has indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Last Friday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And our case manager, Ms. Cmeric, in fact sent an e-mail in relation to that on the 16th, reminding the Prosecution of that, and the deadline. But we haven't at this stage, prior to coming into court, received a response in relation to that as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not in the loop on this particular dialogue between the Defence and the Prosecution. I will look into it during the recess, and I will try to get back to you either today or tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Chamber could be informed about -- well, first of all, of course, the reason of the delay, because it has been -- the parties have been instructed according to this schedule, and at least when we have resolved it, because I take it it's not very dramatic if it would take one or two more days, but let's try to resolve the matter, because there are a lot of other exhibits still to be taken positions upon and we'd like to do that all in once. Then, apart from this one procedural issue, are there other procedural issues that have to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Your Honour. In relation to the next witness, I've indicated to Ms. Karagiannakis that I have an objection in relation to some terminology that was used in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis has dealt with that, and I think that issue is settled between the parties. That just leaves one remaining aspect, because the term is actually used -- it's an overarching term that's used in paragraph 20 of the statement, expelled, and in the circumstances, I'd be objecting to the use of an overarching term of that nature as opposed to the eliciting of evidence from the witness in relation to the direct evidence that the witness can give of those particular matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our position is it should remain in the statement. I intend to examine the witness on what he means when he uses that term so that the Court and the Defence can understand precisely the basis for his use of that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The words do not appear in the summary?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I have excluded them from the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have excluded them from the summary. Does that mean that the summary I have on my desk is already the amended one? Where did it appear, so that I can ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appeared in the last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's replaced by what word now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: It would be -- delete that word and then end to the end of the sentence "that left after the shelling."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means then -- yes. Okay. Then we hear that from you because I take it that the summary to the extent is used as an 89(F) summary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: It also appears, Your Honour, at the -- in the last paragraph of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And it reads: "And the expulsion of." Those words are deleted, replaced with "and," and then after "Muslims" insert the word "leaving."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Will the Chamber receive an amend the copy of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Ms. Loukas, having heard the response of the Prosecution where Ms. Karagiannakis explained to us that she'll further explore the matter of the wordings in the first line of paragraph 20, the Chamber sees at this moment no reason to not to -- not to admit the statement into evidence under 89(F), but we'll hear what the witness will testify about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That just leaves one final matter that I want to deal with at this stage. Your Honours will recall that on the 4th of October, the week before last, I did indicate that I would be proposing to file to withdraw, in light of the inadequate time granted to the Defence and in the circumstances, the question of a fair trial. I can indicate, of course, Your Honour, we were dealing with witnesses that particular week, and last week, as Your Honours are well aware, have been dealing with 92 bis, and I'll be dealing with the witnesses this week, but I propose to be in a position to file the necessary documentation next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the necessary documentation. That is documentation in relation to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Question of withdrawal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Question of withdrawal. Of course, I couldn't say that the Chamber is looking forward to see it. I would say rather the opposite. But I do understand that it's not -- it's still in your mind and that you'll file the request and what needs to support the request --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- soon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just as Your Honour is not looking forward to receiving it, I'm not looking forward to drafting it, but that's another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in that respect, the feelings are concurrent.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: One further matter, Your Honour. My niece is currently staying with me. She is 15 years of age, and I wanted her to come to court today, but apparently she is 15 years and eight months and you have to be 16. So I have to make a formal application to Your Honours so that my niece can come to court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would think for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am -- we'll have to consider that. Have you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond exchanged views with the Prosecution on what will be the subject of -- I do understand that four months is not a lot of difference. I mean, 16, 15 years and 8 months, but, on the other hand, you'll understand what is our only concern about that is not to expose persons under a certain age to -- especially when it comes to testimony which might be shocking.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I do not know exactly what evidence we'll hear tomorrow. Of course, I do not know your relative as far as -- I mean, there's quite a variety of -- in this age. I take it, Ms. Loukas, that, first of all, of course, you'll take some responsibility for yourself knowing exactly what it is about. We'll give you a decision, but I'd also like for you to consult with the Prosecution to the extent that the risks are not such that we would later on regret that we allowed her to be present.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But I'm sure we can come to some accommodation in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: One final matter, just briefly. In relation to the witness that is to follow, the next witness, and of course the next witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is a protect witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- is a protected witness. I'll indicate that I have made some objections in relation to that particular statement, because it is a rather long statement and has, in the Defence view, a rather -- certainly a large amount of extraneous material, we would submit, and I've indicated some objections to the Prosecution. I think the Prosecution lawyer handling that particular witness is Mr. Margetts, and I just wanted to place that on the record as well. Because it is a very long statement, almost in the nature of a novella, and in the circumstances, Your Honour, I think requires some streamlining. And I just want to place that on the record that I've made that objection, and I think it's being considered at this time by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll see then what remains finally. Yes, having dealt with these procedural issues, on the list, Ms. Karagiannakis, I do not find your name as the one who would examine the next witness, but you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I will be doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're ready to start it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures, then. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vatric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration prior to giving evidence in this court. The text of this solemn declaration is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vatric, you'll first be examined by Ms. Karagiannakis, counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be shown his statement dated 21 January 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that statement would have Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vatric, do you recognise this statement as a statement that you have given previously to representatives of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review this statement before today's court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 19 of the statement. In that paragraph, in the fourth full sentence, reference is made to the Hotel Trnovo. Should that reference read "Hotel Treskavica"?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. There is no such thing as a Hotel Trnovo. It's Hotel Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now with that correction, are you satisfied that this statement is correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I certainly agree that it is truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I propose to read a summary of the statement before asking the witness any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vatric, Ms. Karagiannakis will read a summary of your statement because we might not go through all the details of your statement and focus on specific parts of it, but in order for the public to know what your statement is about, she'll read the summary. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: From February 1991, the witness was a member of the Executive Board of Trnovo. This body constituted the municipal government. He provides evidence about the political situation and personalities in the municipality during 1991 and 1992, including the SDS municipal leaders: Radivoje Draskovic and Glisa Simanic. The witness testifies as to the build-up to and subsequent shelling and takeover of Trnovo and its aftermath, including the number of casualties and the destination and numbers of the Muslim population that left after the shelling. All of the officials bodies of the municipality had Serb bodies elected as shadow organisations. A Serb MUP was created and located in the cultural centre, over which the Serb flag was raised. Three checkpoints were established in Trnovo in March 1992. The White Eagles were manning a checkpoint in the first half of April 1992. They stopped him and another Muslim and, after checking their identity cards, they were not allowed to go to Trnovo town after that. On the 1st of May, 1992, the witness returned to Trnovo by an alternative route and found that the municipal organisation had been split; a coordination body between Muslims and Serbs had been established; and Serbs were wearing uniforms and trenches were being dug around the town. On 24 May 1992, a municipal War Presidency was formed and the Serbs were invited to join; however, they declined to do so and withdrew from all public institutions. Seven days before the attack on Trnovo, Serbs started moving around the town and tanks appeared. The day before the attack Serbs started leaving the town, and the witness's Serb secretary warned him to take care of himself because "something very serious is about to happen." The town was shelled the next day, 31 May 1992, resulting in five deaths, the capture and disappearance of 14 people, and approximately two and a half thousand Muslims leaving to various locations. The witness was responsible for the accommodation of the Muslims that left. Upon his return to Trnovo town, he observed that many houses had been burned or damaged and the mosque has been pulled down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vatric, can you tell the Court what position you held in the municipality of Trnovo during 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I was secretary of the secretariat for economic and financial Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond matters, as well as general social affairs. So this was a very comprehensive secretariat. At the same time, I was a member of the Executive Council of the municipality from 1991 onwards and after the war too, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What's the role of the Executive Board of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board of the municipality of Trnovo is practically the executive that is then answerable to the Assembly of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was the population of Trnovo municipality, approximately, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Trnovo had a population of about 7.000 on an area of 450 square kilometres. So it was very sparsely populated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court the ethnic breakdown of that population?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: 70 per cent of the population was Bosniak Muslim, and 30 per cent were Serbs. There were very few Croats, hardly any, perhaps one or two per cent, but certainly not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the population of Trnovo town was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: The town of Trnovo is a very small town, very small. The population was about 2.000 to 2.500, at maximum. That is the town itself. And around Trnovo are villages that are not really villages per se but part of the town, but all things considered, the population would not exceed 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic breakdown of the population of Trnovo town?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I think that Trnovo itself had a population that was about 50 or 55 per cent Bosniak Muslim. The rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the map Sarajevo within BiH, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P323.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And could the map, please, be placed on the ELMO so that the witness can mark it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain Trnovo's position in respect of the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Trnovo lies to the south-east of Sarajevo. It is one -- it used to be one of the ten municipalities of Sarajevo before the war. As I said, it stretches over an area of 450 square kilometres to the south-east of Sarajevo. And it is across the communication line to Foca, from Sarajevo, and through to the eastern Herzegovinian access to sea and up to the north-east, to Visegrad, and then, of course, to the south-west, to Montenegro. So it is the south-eastern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court the main roads that provide access to the sea from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are two main roads linking Sarajevo with the sea. This is the M-17, Sarajevo-Konjic-Mostar-Ploce, and a second road going from Sarajevo across Trnovo and Foca and on to Gacko, Bileca until Dubrovnik. These were the two main roads in the direction of the sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could you please take a pen and just trace the road through Konjic and Mostar to the sea and mark that with the number 1. And then trace the other road you described on the map and mark that with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: The road number 1 and this is the road number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, does road number 2 actually pass through the -- through Trnovo town itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It passes through the centre of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The map can be put away. Were there any JNA barracks in Trnovo prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No, not in the area of Trnovo municipality. There were no JNA barracks. There were just two facilities of a different character on the slopes of the Jahorina mountain, but they were not the typical military facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Where were the nearest JNA barracks to Trnovo municipality before the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: The closest barracks were Kalinovik, Hadzici and Lukavica. I think those were the closest barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did the JNA barracks at Kalinovik have artillery?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. These were the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army that had long been in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Just going back to the issue of the two roads that provide access to the sea from Sarajevo. You told us about a road going through Konjic and Mostar. Now, during 1992, which forces controlled the areas through which that road, which is marked as number 1, controlled it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that question, I think it probably needs a little bit more delineation as to time in 1992 we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: From April 1992, which forces controlled that road to the sea going through Konjic and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, Ilidza and Hadzici were under the control of the Serb forces. So this particular road had been severed, leaving from Sarajevo. Now, when we talk about the roads to the sea, I wouldn't know which forces held which areas, but I think that near Mostar, there was one section of the road that wasn't passable, that was actually occupied. But in Ilidza and Hadzici, the road had been blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And which forces controlled the municipalities of Konjic and Mostar at that time? If you know.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Konjic was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was around April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And Mostar?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about Mostar. I wasn't in Mostar at the time. But there were forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the HVO, and of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I wouldn't really know which sections of the road belonged to which forces, because I was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I just want to move on to a number of events that you describe in your statement that occurred before the 31st of May. In paragraph -- I'll ask you to look at paragraph 8 of your statement. There you say that during 1991, you noticed changes taking place, and I quote: "I noticed it first through the actions of these two colleagues," and there you're referring to Mr. Adzic and Mr. Boskovic. Could you tell the Court what changes you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: These were mostly changes at the workplace. These were two colleagues of ours working together with us with the Executive Board. They were young people who did their job in a very proper way prior to the war, in a way that was in no way different from our working style. At the beginning of 1991, you could already feel them being distanced in terms of the decision-making process, the process of -- the decision taking wasn't as easy as before. They did not state their positions very clearly as before. So you couldn't really say what it was, tangibly, that was different with the two colleagues, but you could feel the difference in their conduct at the meetings, where they would tend to postpone certain matters for some later stage. We noticed perhaps most of all that they were in a way losing their autonomy in what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You said there they would tend to postpone certain matters for some later stage. What sort of matters are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Generally, the Executive Board discussed a number of issues of the local character pertaining to the municipality, utilities, schooling, and so on. Since Trnovo was a local community, it did not have its own sources, but depended on the funds from Sarajevo. That is why we mainly dealt with local issues, road-building, infrastructure, and so on. These were issues that could not be considered major issues for such a small community and that would not really lead to any great changes in the community. So issues of local infrastructure, education, companies active in the area, whereas other matters were mostly related to the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know which party these two people belonged to? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: They were nominated on behalf of the SDS, so they were members of the SDS and were designated by the party as the candidates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you please have a look at paragraph 10 of your statement. You say there in the first line: "Further developments were a reflection of the developments in Sarajevo and East Bosnia rather than the situation in Trnovo itself." Could you please explain what you mean by that statement.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Trnovo was a small town, a community where people knew each other. There were no conflicts locally. And the events of the time were actually a reflection of what was going on at the higher level in Sarajevo, which was the political centre of the country, where the political conflicts could be seen aired on the TV and in the mass media, which of course had an impact on Trnovo. And already in the first half of 1992, in Eastern Bosnia, there were conflicts in place. People started moving towards Central Bosnia, and the population leaving Foca and other places over there passed through Trnovo. And that's what I meant by saying this. Of course, inevitably, this disrupted the relations in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was the -- insofar as you know, what was the population leaving Foca and passing through Trnovo, what ethnicity was that population?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know their numbers, but a lot of people passed through Trnovo in 1992. There were large columns of people, of Muslims, from Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, could you have a look at paragraph 11. There you say that you heard about the Crisis Staff. When and how did you hear about the establishment of the SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I personally did not know when the Crisis Staff - that is, the SDS Assembly - was established. I wasn't politically active in either of the parties, so I wasn't a member of the forum of political parties. But there were some indications pointing to the fact that such institutions had been established in Trnovo as well. This typical period, winter from 2001 to 2002, when certain staffs and assemblies were established, it's very difficult for me to specify the dates. But the end of 1991 up to the spring of 1992, this became apparent due to the different signs that were placed on the institutions, people claiming to be members of different institutions. All the issues that I could notice while discharging my regular duties at the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How did you first hear about the creation of the SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I learnt it from colleagues and I could see some places where flags were hoisted where there were no flags before, next to the Hotel Treskavica, culture centre, and other places where there were Serb companies. So I did not know precisely that the Assembly had been established, but I could notice it by these new manifestations and of course from conversations with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you said two things. You said that you heard about the creation of an SDS Crisis Staff and then you heard about a Serb assembly. Now, I'm asking you now about the SDS Crisis Staff just to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, what's actually stated at paragraph 11 is: "I had no personal knowledge of the establishment of the SDS Crisis Staff. I had heard about it, but my only knowledge was hearsay and I do not feel competent to comment on these matters. I did not attend meetings where subjects like this were discussed." So the paraphrasing that Ms. Karagiannakis gave that particular aspect needs some correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm happy to quote the precise passage to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Have a look at paragraph 11 and have a look at the first and second sentences of that paragraph. I'm going to read them out to you: "I had no personal knowledge of the establishment of the SDS Crisis Staff. I had heard about it," and then the sentence continues. Would you just tell the Court when and how you heard about it.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: In any case, I wasn't officially informed about the establishment of such a body, although I was an official of the municipality, and it would have been quite normal for me to be informed officially of it in normal times. The colleagues I heard this from were people who knew of this because they were members of other political parties and were in communication with these people. Mehmed Mulaosmanovic was the president of the municipality of Trnovo. He had this information, and I can tell you that I heard it from him, but I could not, of course, say who the others were that I also heard it from. But he was one of them, and he was an official there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And do you remember when you heard it from Mr. Mulaosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: As I've said, it's very difficult to date this. I really have to speak of the period of the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. I cannot be certain in any way about the dates, and that's why I would like to keep it at just dating it to the period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, I'm a bit confused. Perhaps you could clarify that for me. In paragraph 11 of the statement, a distinction is made between the SDS Crisis Staff and -- well, at least, I don't know whether it's a distinction. SDS Crisis Staff and Serb Assembly, which seems to be two different bodies. Whereas in the answer of the witness on page 17, line 2, it reads: "I personally did not know when the Crisis Staff, that is, the SDS Assembly, was established." Could you clarify whether we are talking about one or about two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm now going to move on to the issue of the Serb Assembly. There was some confusion in I think what the witness understood and said. That's why I asked him specifically about the Crisis Staff in the last set of questions, and now I'll ask him about the Serb Assembly and he'll be able to hopefully clarify it for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps you could confront him with his previous answer where he seems to put them together. It's page 17, line 2, at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, I don't have that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read it for you. Perhaps I could ask a clarification. Mr. Vatric, you said in your testimony a couple of minutes ago: "I personally did not know when the Crisis Staff, that is, the SDS Assembly, was established." From your written statement, it appears that -- at least, that's how I read it - that the Crisis Staff is not exactly the same as the SDS Assembly. Could you please clarify whether you consider them to be two different bodies or one body, and to explain to us what, if different bodies, what the one was and what the other was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think these are two distinct bodies, although I could not really speak about their jurisdictions, what their purview was. But of course, the Assembly was supposed to be the official representative body of the municipality of Trnovo that was supposed to assume all the tasks that the legally elected assembly discharged. Whereas the Crisis Staff, according to what I inferred from what I knew, because I could not really firsthand have any experience of it, was an organ formed by the SDS to operate at the time. So these should be two distinct bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: At paragraph 11 of your statement, you say, and I'll read out the sentence to you: "I heard that a Serb Assembly had been officially elected, but I did not attend any of its meetings." Could you please tell the Court how and when you heard about the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond election of a Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Again, I heard this from my colleagues in the municipality, having been a member of the Executive Board, and my colleagues having been members of the different political parties, I learnt it from conversations with them. Again, I cannot say whether it was the beginning of 1992 or the end of 1991, but it was wintertime, and I was told that a second assembly had been established, assembly of Trnovo, that was supposed to continue functioning. Of course, I did not really think about it afterwards, because I just thought it was a regular body.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Then you go on to say in paragraph 11: "In 1992, the Hotel Treskavica was the place where they had their official meetings." Now, could you please tell the Court who or what you mean when you say "they" in that sentence.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Of course. They were the Serbian Democratic Party that assumed the political role, formed its parallel organs. It was seated in the area of Hotel Treskavica in Trnovo and that is why their meetings were mostly held in Hotel Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you see the SDS members gathering for those meetings?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I saw a number of times the SDS people leaving to Hotel Treskavica. I was, however, never there. I don't know whether they held their meetings there, or what they were doing there. I just saw them going to one of the rooms in Hotel Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And when was the first time you saw them going there?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say when it was that I first saw them there, because it is true that Serbs did meet in Hotel Treskavica. And I saw politicians meeting there. I saw them in 1991 and in 1992. I cannot, though, give you a specific date. But it was really often that I would see these people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Right at the end of that paragraph, you say, and I quote: "I know that one day the Serb MUP was created and located in the culture centre. They raised the Serb flag over the building." Now, when did you see -- sorry. How do you know that the Serb MUP was created and located in the culture centre?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: It was easy to come by that information because there were people of Serb nationality working in MUP who separated themselves and were stationed at the cultural centre that was just being built. The building works were nearing the end there. And they hoisted their flag there, which meant that they were forming a new institution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the end part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: But I apologise, because of course 15 years have elapsed, and that is quite a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vatric, I hear and see on my screen that the interpreter could not hear the last part of your answer to that question. Could you please repeat it. And perhaps if you could lean a little bit more closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I know that people of Serb ethnicity, police officers, used to work at the Trnovo police station. They left the Trnovo police station and then were stationed at the cultural centre, which was supposed to be the general community centre. They hoisted their flag there and established a new institution, and this was common knowledge. The only thing I cannot tell you is the specific date. But I believe it was in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that they raised a Serb flag over the building. Can you describe what that flag looked like.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: This was the SDS flag, with the four S's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, could you please -- I refer you now to paragraph 13 of your statement. Just a general question in relation to this paragraph and then a more specific one. Now, you mentioned that Radivoje Draskovic, and in paragraph 9 of your statement you say that Draskovic had been the former president of the Executive Board before the elections. And then full stop: "At that time I believe he was the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS." Do you know of any other SDS positions that Mr. Draskovic held?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections in 1990, Mr. Draskovic left the position of the president of the Executive Board of Trnovo. In 1992, he became the president of the SDS party in Trnovo, but I know of -- I do not know of any other function that he discharged except for this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned in paragraph 13 Glisa Simovic. What party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Glisa Simanic was also a member of the League of Communists before these events occurred, and then he did join the ranks of the SDS and pursued the SDS policy. I do not know whether he was formally a member, but he was the -- later on also there on behalf of MUP in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the last line of paragraph 13 you say: "Glisa Simanic was also a former communist." You've explained that to us. And then you go on to say: "And had a high position in the municipality of Trnovo for many years." Could you tell the Court what high position in the municipality he had?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Since he spent a number of years in Trnovo and in communist times, the officials would merely change positions from MUP, then on to the Committee of the League of Communists, so he basically held all the leading, different leading positions in the municipality of Trnovo. Later on, he was in the town MUP and the republican MUP. I don't know which positions he held, but these were mainly leadership positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraphs -- you don't have to look at them, but I'm just summarising. Paragraphs 12 and 15, you discover -- sorry, you discuss the establishment of barricades and checkpoints in March. Now, were there any negotiations that you know about that related to the topic of barricades or checkpoints in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: The month of March was the month of barricades in Sarajevo and in all the Sarajevo municipalities, including Trnovo. There were checkpoints, barricades, in a number of places. There was a series of negotiations run by the president of municipality, Mr. Mulaosmanovic, with representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party. I wasn't personally involved in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Which members of the Serbian Democratic Party negotiated with Mr. Mulaosmanovic about barricades and checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Draskovic, as president of the SDS, for the most part, and Mr. Simanic. But I don't know in which capacity he was there at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just want to leave a marker there, Your Honour, just in relation to the question of which members of the party negotiated there. When the witness has already given an answer that: "I wasn't involved in the negotiations." The following question should probably have a proviso to your knowledge in view of the previous answer. But I'm putting a marker there. Obviously the question has been answered now. But I think it's important the questions are confined to the witness's specific, direct knowledge of matters, where they can be, and particularly where he said: "I have no direct involvement." Perhaps a little bit more care there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We took notice of your marker, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How do you know that Mr. Draskovic and Mr. Simanic engaged in negotiations with Mr. Mulaosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mulaosmanovic's office was right next door to my office in the municipality, so I was there, so I knew about it, and I heard about it from the president of the municipality. It was easy to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And what happened as a result of these negotiations, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: After these negotiations -- well, I don't know whether these negotiations contributed to this, but anyway, the barricades were removed throughout Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did barricades, checkpoints, subsequently reappear at any stage in Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: In the month of April, I could not come to Trnovo. I lived in Hrasnica. So I had to travel through Vojkovici and other neighbourhoods. So I simply couldn't make it to Trnovo. A month later I came to Trnovo via Igman. Of course in the area of Treskavica, I came across a checkpoint, a barricade, a roadblock, where I was asked to show an ID and then they let me pass because they knew what my job was. And then again I saw roadblocks in Trnovo. As for the road between Sarajevo and Trnovo, I knew about that because before, even on the 2nd of April I think, I think it was the 1st or 2nd of April, that was the last time when I was cautioned about this, that we could no longer go to Trnovo that way. So this is March and then April and then the third time I went back to Trnovo was in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You say you were asked to show -- I'm trying to read your answer to you and ask for clarification. "A month later I came back to Trnovo via Igman. In the area of Treskavica, I came across a barricade, checkpoint, roadblocks, where I was asked to show ID and then they let me pass." Now, who was manning that roadblock or checkpoint or barricade?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: My briefest possible answer would be that these were paramilitaries, members of paramilitary formations, mostly ethnic Serbs. I could not call them a military formation. They wore uniforms that belonged to reservists of the former Yugoslav People's Army and they also wore civilian clothes. So as a person who worked in the system of government, I can say that for me they were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And when you went back to Trnovo town itself in May did you see any barricades in Trnovo town itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Not in the town of Trnovo itself. There weren't any barricades. It was my impression, and that is the way it was, in fact, that by then, Trnovo was already divided along ethnic lines. In the area of the municipality and in the area where there were Bosniaks, there were hardly any Serbs left, and the other way around. So barricades were no longer needed, as Trnovo had already been divided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned division. Could you look at paragraph 17 of your statement. I think it's the fourth sentence you said: "When I returned to Trnovo, I found all the organisations split into separate organisations." And later on you say Trnovo was divided. Could you explain what you mean by organisations split into separate organisations.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Of course I can explain. It's very simple. State institutions. There was the municipality that did not function, and the municipality building was closed down. Then the defence department that was within the municipality. It no longer had any ethnic Serbs there. Then the MUP, the security station. It was already divided into two MUPs. There was only one coordinating body that was operating, and that was a peace council established by the citizens. They were debating things and probably trying to keep the peace, if possible. However, there were no other state organisations or social organisations in Trnovo. There was also the health centre. It was an institution of a kind too. But I could not say whether it was divided or not, because it involved professionals, people who did their actual work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You said in your answer that there was only one coordination body that was operating and that was a peace council established by the citizens. Were any of the elected representatives of the SDS or the SDA on that peace council?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it was constituted, how it was established, whether it was political parties that had put up their candidates for it. But if I look at the people who were actually on the council, I could not say whether it was the political parties who established this or not. Knowing Mr. Boro Popovic, Mr. Mulaomerovic, they were not really political party oriented people and they were on this council. I think that these were individuals who were trying to maintain good neighbourly relations, or rather, peace in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please look at paragraph 19 of your statement. You say: "The seven days before the attack I was in Trnovo. There were Serb military formations walking around Trnovo." Can you tell us whether these formation -- whether these formations were armed or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I can. These were formations that wore uniforms of the reserve force of the army of Yugoslavia. They had insignia which were no longer insignia of the Yugoslav army. Some of them were armed too, of course. I slept in Trnovo then, so during those eight days, I was in Trnovo round the clock. During the night, I would often hear gunfire. During the day, one could see people moving about in Trnovo, and one could realise that something was going on. All of it gave the feeling of something military that was going on, and that turned out to be true later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you saw insignia. Are you able to describe what that insignia was?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should call it the times of folklore in Sarajevo and Trnovo. From nationalist insignia to insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army. I don't know now. I mean, I can't tell anything more specific now, but there was the Serb flag, no longer the flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this meant that it was mono-ethnic. At checkpoints, I often saw insignia that belonged to the war before that, that is to say, the Sajkaca caps, the cockades, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Further on in that part of your statement, you say: "Tanks appeared in front of..." what you corrected to read as "Hotel Treskavica." Do you know who those tanks belonged to?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact who had the tanks: The Yugoslav People's Army. They left them behind and they made them available to the forces in Trnovo which - I emphasise this once again - were, in my opinion, paramilitaries. They were not within the Yugoslav People's Army. I did my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army myself, and the army never resorted to that. So these were tanks and equipment that remained in the area and that was there in front of the Hotel Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on in that paragraph, you say that during that period, and I quote you: "I then saw that Serb people were leaving the town." Can you please tell us when you saw that.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: It was on a Friday, the end of May, when working hours were over. Everybody saw this commotion around town and we saw the Serb population leaving. However, to tell you the truth, this was not a special type of signal to me at the time, because people were moving about all the time anyway. However, later on this proved to be the case on Saturday as well. So by the time the attack on Trnovo took place, practically the entire Serb population had left Trnovo and they were taken to Treskavica and Tosici, and after that Trnovo was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic make-up of the village of Tosici is?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Mono-ethnic. Only two or three Bosniak houses, I think. So the population were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You then report a conversation you had, and I'll just read that out to you: "A Serb woman who was a secretary at our office said to me as she left that day: Take care of yourself, boss, something very serious is about to happen." Can you tell the Court when she said that to you and what you did in response.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: To be quite sincere, it wasn't really a conversation; it was a single sentence that I happened to recall later and to realise what it actually meant. At any rate, everything that happened in Trnovo during those few days probably led to that, the fact that this sentence was something that I was told, and it probably conveyed a kind of message because on the second or on the third day, Trnovo was actually shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, the last line of that paragraph is that the town of -- the town was shelled that day, the 31st of May, 1992. Did you actually -- were you actually in the town on that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was not in town on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: So how do you know the town was shelled that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in the area of municipality of Trnovo. Trnovo is the very centre of the municipality, and everybody knows what's going on in town. My colleagues were in town, and they were there throughout. So on Friday afternoon, I left town. I went to see my family, or rather, one of my children, and the next day the town was attacked. Of course, when I heard about this, I set out for Trnovo straight away and I saw this with my very own eyes, because the shelling continued. It wasn't stopped at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see where the shelling was originating from?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Of course. It wasn't hard to see. Shells were coming from the area of Rogoj and the Hotel Treskavica. So Rogoj would be the right way of putting it. This is a pass between Kalinovik and Trnovo, a mountain pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 20, you state: "After the attack on the 31st of May, the Muslim population was expelled from Trnovo." Why do you say that the population was expelled?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I don't think there is any other expression in the Bosnian language but to say that you were expelled if somebody made you leave by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Then you go on to say in paragraph 20 that your duty was to -- immediate duty was to take care of these people. Then you mention the numbers of 1.000 to 1.500 Bosniaks, and then a further thousand people who had been previously displaced from Foca. Can you tell the Court approximately what percentage of those people were women, and children, and elderly people?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: These were primarily families that lived in the town of Trnovo, so there were women and children and elderly people there; adults too, of course. It would be hard for me to give any percentages now, because at that time there were no splits among the population. Everybody had to leave Trnovo under the shells and under the fire. So practically no one stayed behind in Trnovo. Everybody left. I did not go into the percentages even at that time, how many women, how many children, although it is always possible to deduce that figure from the relative figures that exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, the last part of paragraph 20, I'll quote this. You say: "On the first day of the war, five citizens of Trnovo were killed by the shelling and 14 were captured. We do not know what happened to any of those 14 who have never been seen again." Now, how did you come to know about these events?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I was in the village of Trebecaj for the most part. That is two kilometres away from the centre of Trnovo. So it wasn't hard to hear about all of this from the people who were leaving Trnovo, about who got killed, where shells fell, et cetera. I believe, though, that there are some accurate records as well. Perhaps people who worked for the health services or people who were engaged in these efforts later. I know about these 14 people because there was an employee of the municipality of Trnovo among them, and he lived in the neighbourhood where the Treskavica Hotel was. I know that he was taken away because his wife got out the following day and she told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And insofar as you knew or --

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, insofar as you knew or were told by the refugees, what was the ethnicity of the people that were killed and the five people that were killed and the 14 people that were captured?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks, of course. It was the Bosniak population that was leaving Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was the name of the employee of the municipality who was among the 14 people?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Munib Velic was his name. He was a land surveyor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, before I give you an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, I would ask one question to the witness at this moment. When asked why you used the word that Muslims were expelled, you explained that they had to leave by force. Could you explain a little bit more what do you mean by that, how this actually took place. What force was exercised? How precisely that went on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the force came from artillery weapons. The town was shelled. The unprotected civilian population in Trnovo was shelled, and this went on incessantly. That's what my colleague Mr. Durmo told me when he got out of Trnovo. There was this physical attack against Trnovo. And there was no other way of protecting the population but getting them out to the neighbouring villages. That's what they did. They left during the night. They went from one house to the other, depending on who managed to do what. So it was direct force that was used, coming from artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I do understand that the Serbian population of Trnovo had left already. Did they return at any later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They returned immediately, as soon as the Bosniak population and police got out of Trnovo. I think that there were also direct conflicts with the police. However, there were very few of them, but that is what the people who stayed in Trnovo said. There were no Bosniaks left in Trnovo, and the Serbs returned a few days later. I don't know exactly when this happened, because I was no longer in Trnovo myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Bosniaks could not have returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for what reason? Could you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it had already turned into a war, and there were war operations that were going on already. Combat lines were established. So the population left. We're talking about the end of May 1992, when Bosnia-Herzegovina, Trnovo included, had become a battleground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that what you understand by being expelled is that they first had to flee due to the shelling and were not able later on to return because of the war operations that would not allow them to return. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is a correct understanding, but it's not only that they could not return due to war operations, but also because the authorities that were in place in Trnovo did not even try to call them to come back to Trnovo. I'm referring to the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. Ms. Loukas, I'm wondering whether it would not be better to start cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that's a good idea. And I can indicate that I won't be that long with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean that the next witness should be available already this afternoon. Ms. Karagiannakis, is there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the only witness that is ready to testify today. His testimony has gone much faster than what we anticipated. The other witness only arrived today -- sorry, yesterday and is only speaking to the attorney in charge of leading his evidence today. And I understand those discussions are still ongoing. And he will not be ready to come on after this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Karagiannakis, from a point of view of planning, of course, I mean, you're the only one who was aware how much this witness would approximately take. That would be less than one hour and a half, under the 60 per cent rule. It's a bit surprising that the Prosecution did not prepare for the next witness to be present. We have had similar problems of planning and logistics before. If we try to move forward as efficiently as possible, this preferably should not happen. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Vatric, please be seated. You'll now be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence, Ms. Loukas. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vatric, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just prior to the break, His Honour, the Presiding Judge, was asking you some questions in relation to paragraph 20, you'll recall, of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. I think it was yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And just going to paragraph 11 of your statement, you indicated there that you had no personal knowledge of the establishment of the SDS Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: As far as my personal knowledge goes, that relates to the place and date of the establishment of crisis staffs. Later on, when they became active, I referred to the Crisis Staff that operated in Trnovo municipality, to the extent that I heard something from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. And of course, Mr. Vatric, the situation is, in terms of what you've placed in your statement and in the way that you've given your evidence today, you're careful to indicate what you know on the basis of your personal knowledge and what you hear from others; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've done my best to make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, you're being, of course, fairly, and importantly, careful not to speculate; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. I've done my best to recall and say anything that I can be certain of.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just getting back to paragraph 20 of your statement. His Honour, the Presiding Judge, asked you about the use of the term "expelled" there in the first sentence, and you've given evidence in relation to that in answer to His Honour's question. So I don't propose to ask you anything further about that particular sentence. Just going down, further down paragraph 20, I think it's the fourth sentence, the sentence that begins: "At the beginning, it was the population who lived in the town who were displaced." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, you used the term "displaced" in that sentence; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then in the following sentence, the sentence that begins: "The second part of a population," you use the term "expelled" in that next sentence; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in the following sentence, that begins: "There were about a further thousand people who had been previously displaced," again you used, twice in that sentence, the term "displaced"; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I often use the terms "displaced" and "expelled." And to answer this right away, perhaps not the right term was used for a given category that your question relates to. I was talking about those displaced from Trnovo, because I knew that they were -- or rather, expelled, those expelled from Trnovo, because I know that they were expelled. And when I speak of those who were displaced, I mean the people that I'm not sure of whether they left Trnovo before the shelling or after. And sometimes I really use the terms "displaced" and "expelled" without really thinking about the term that I'm using. But you're free to ask a specific question and I'll try to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you concede that you have on occasion used the terms "expelled" and "displaced" interchangeably; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: That's what the text reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to the next part of the paragraph 20, when you talk about the first day of the war, and you indicate that five citizens were killed. The source of your knowledge there is, I take it, not direct knowledge but what you've heard from others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And again, similarly, in relation to I think the 14 people you've described as being captured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I know that 14 people were taken away. I know the man who was in the group. Of course, I wasn't there. I learnt it from others. I learnt it from Mr. and Mrs. -- I learnt it from Mrs. Velic, who was there when her husband was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to some more general matters in relation to Trnovo. Are you aware that the office of the SDS Municipal Board was next to the office of the SDA Municipal Board? In fact, they were in the same building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The offices of the political parties originally used to be in a building next to the municipality building, and each party had one office.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think they were basically separated by a partition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I don't know which material was used, but the offices were separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: They were right next door to each other virtually; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. They used a common corridor to enter their offices respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to Trnovo: You're aware, of course, that both -- there were both Muslim and Serb crisis staffs. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, I said that I did not take any direct part in the activities of any political parties, nor was I a member of any body. I was asked about the Serbian Democratic Party. Of course, probably following these events, different political parties responded in their own ways, but I would not be able to say anything substantially about their political activities, apart from what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, on another topic: Were you aware in early March of 1992 of barricades being set up by both Serbs and by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I was -- I did not learn this, but I rather saw it with my own eyes as I was going to Trnovo from Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in relation to Danilo Goljanin - I hope you'll forgive my pronunciation - he was not a member of the SDS, was he, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's a little difficult, unfortunately, because the lectern is rather large and positioning the microphone appropriately has become an issue. But I'll move it across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm confident that you'll manage, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Were you aware whether or not Danilo Goljanin was a member of the SDS or do you have no knowledge of that matter?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this. I know of the family name Goljanin, but I know nothing of the activities of Danilo Goljanin himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to -- are you aware of a gentleman by the name of Edhem Gorinak [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Edhem Gorinak.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Edhem Gorinak. He was the chief of the police administration in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of his being involved in setting up barricades and seizing vehicles, activities of that nature, during March 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to round about April 1992, somewhere between the 16th and the 19th of April 1992: Were you aware of a group of Muslims attacking a mixed police patrol and killing three policemen, one of which was a Serb and two of whom were Muslims? Were you aware of an event of that nature?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was in Hrasnica. Therefore, I was not in Trnovo. Later on, I naturally heard that an incident had taken place, but I do not know the reasons lying behind it, nor who fired or who was the victim. I only heard about it. But throughout April I was in Hrasnica and not in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've already given evidence about the splitting of the police force between the Serbs and the Muslims. Are you aware of the fact that the weapons actually stayed with the Muslims when the Serb policemen went to the cultural house of Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I don't think the police station was divided along the -- between the Bosniaks and Serbs. It was rather the ethnic Serb members that left the public security station Trnovo and moved to other premises. Now, what they actually took along with them or what they left behind, I am not aware of. So there was no division. It was the ethnic Serbs who abandoned the regular police station in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of whether or not, in late March 1992, Trnovo being cut off from Sarajevo, round about that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I passed along this road. I can't remember clearly, but I think I used the road from Sarajevo through Hrasnica to Trnovo until April, and the entire road to Trnovo was passable. Now, whether it was cut off, I suppose it would be cut off for the regular traffic. If you have some blockades or points blocking it, then they would probably be visible. However, I was able to pass along that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to round about when that road was cut off?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in early April, when I was cautioned about the checkpoint in Krupac. I was warned, actually, by members of a paramilitary group there that we would not be able to pass. There was Miralem Ramic with me there, president of the Executive Board, with me in the car. So for me, that's when the road was already cut off. Whether there was anyone else going -- using this road, I know that after the 6th of April, nobody could use the road any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Are you aware of round about the 31st of May, 1992 Muslims capturing a group of approximately 25 to 28 Serbs in the region of Trnovo and Ljuta?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't know. Ljuta belongs to Kalinovik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And are you aware of Serbs fleeing homes around that time as a result of that event? I mean, if you know, yes; if you don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Trnovo, the municipality of Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Leaving as a result of this incident in relation to some Muslims capturing some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of the Serbian population being on the move in Trnovo municipality in March and April, because before May, nothing significant happened in our municipality, not even in May, until the attack on Trnovo itself was there anybody on the move, because both the Serbian and Bosniak population stayed at their homes until the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you're not aware of Serbs leaving the region of Trnovo and Ljuta as a result of this capture by Muslims of a certain group of Serbs? That's correct, isn't it? You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No. There was absolutely nobody leaving the municipality of Trnovo, be it the Serbs or Bosniaks, until the end of May 1992, or perhaps something took place that I was not aware of. But neither ethnicities left the municipality. The first wave of people leaving was following the attack on Trnovo on the 31st of May. And this is also true for the ethnic Serbs who stayed in their homes. It was the population living in the town proper of Trnovo who started leaving the area once they came under attack, and I emphasise once again: Ljuta was not included into the Trnovo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, on or about the 3rd or 4th of June, 1992, were you aware of Muslim attacks on Serb villages at all?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: This was wartime already. There were military formations there. And I wouldn't know anything specific about either side attacking the other or where it was that the theatre of war came about. It wouldn't really be proper of me to try and answer this question, because I was not informed about any of the formations. I would simply be able to speculate, or, led by you, I wouldn't really know how the armed operations developed. I know that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Territorial Defence organised their units. MUPs had their staffs that were connected to the republic level MUP office. And this was the only thing that I knew. For the rest, it would be merely me conveying to you hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Vatric. You've very much appropriately declined to speculate. I've only got a couple of more aspects to cover with you before we finish. Are you aware of the time when Trnovo was then, I think round about late July, occupied by the Muslims, by the Bosnia-Herzegovinian army, were you aware during that time of approximately 200 Serb civilians being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they cannot hear counsel speaking.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this. I think I returned to Trnovo in August or September, when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whichever way they were called, the Territorial Defence, when they were regrouping, they -- then I returned it Trnovo and I did not find any ethnic Serbs there. I found Trnovo that was destroyed. A part of the population returned there, together with the service, but that's as far as I can tell you. I don't know how many civilians were actually injured, killed. I wouldn't be able to give you the figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And were you aware of the Serb Orthodox church being torched at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: When I returned to Trnovo, both places of worship, the mosque and the church, were damaged. You could see that the church was not functioning, because there were no ethnic Serbs there. And I did notice the damage on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might have a moment, Your Honour. My case manager is trying to get my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Vatric. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Sir, I need a clarification from you. You have said that in the month of May the population was actually divided or separated, if I may put it that way, in such a way that the Muslim population left the Serb-populated areas, and vice versa. You came to the conclusion that this was a reason enough for the checkpoints to be removed, that is to say, there were no more checkpoints, barricades, because there was no need for them and that the population had practically separated, that Serbs no longer lived in Muslim areas, and vice versa. Did you -- is this what you actually said?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No. I did not really mean to say this. What I meant to say was that the population remained in their homes.
