Their workplaces were actually divided, that is, the companies that were around Treskavica Hotel were no longer in operation, which meant that the population did not commute to these factories. The cafes and the social life in Trnovo was already divided along the ethnic lines. Serbs would go to certain cafes and Muslims to others. That's what I meant. And I did not mean that physically they were displaced, that they relocated. They remained in their homes, whereas their work and other activities that required them to move, this was something that was already ethnically divided, and that's the division I had in mind. Now, as for the barricades in the month of May, they were no longer the same as the checkpoints in April and March. They were simply checkpoints controlling the movement, asking people to identify themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not quote your words, or rather, I will, in English. And you explained this by saying that there was a division along the ethnicities. I think you gave a more detailed explanation. You did not really mean to say that there was a clear division between the populations, that it did not come to the situation that the Serbs who lived in Muslim-populated neighbourhoods, that they had left the areas.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: No, this is not what I wanted to say. Neither ethnicity left the areas where they lived, and Trnovo is a mixed community, where people lived in mixed neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why were there barricades in the first place?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Probably to control movement during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But who was in charge of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I would not know who was in charge of the barricades, but the barricades that were put in place in Trnovo, and when I refer to these barricades, I mean the system that was put in place in order to block people from going to their regular jobs and so on, such a system was actually placed by ethnic Serbs. In my opinion, it was the SDS. After that, barricades became a regular practice. Anyone would place a barricade in one's own street in order to control who it was that was entering the street. That's why I call them barricades, roadblocks, that were there in order to thwart the regular course of everybody's day-to-day lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, you said that a certain point in the month of May, and I quote, [In English]: "Barricades were no longer needed." [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, there must have been an authority that took the decision to remove the barricades. Are you aware of this or do you have any information in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I could not really point to a certain authority taking this decision, but I know that there was no need for the checkpoints because all the companies and factories that were active ceased working at that point and nobody had to go there anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well. You told us about paragraph 20 of your statement and about the use of the expression "expelled" and "displaced." You also said that you answered in the affirmative when asked whether you used these terms interchangeably. I'd like to go through it - and perhaps you could take it in front of you - in a bit more in detail. In the first line, you used the word "expelled" from Trnovo. I think you explained to us that that was -- that they had to leave as a result of force. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if we are a few lines further down, it reads: "At the beginning, it was the population who lived in the town who were displaced." Where you used the word "displaced" here, did you refer to displacement as a result of force or not as a result of force?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this paragraph is a bit confusing, as far as this distinction between displaced and expelled is concerned. But perhaps I can explain what I mean when I say "displaced" and when I say "expelled." When I say "expelled," I mean those for whom I know for sure that they were dispelled through the use of physical force, and perhaps those who left homes without the use of any kind of direct force, or at least I don't know about this kind of direct force being used. So it is for the latter group that I use the word "displaced." We had this chain reaction in Trnovo, so people from villages that were not directly attacked by these forces nevertheless left their homes. For me, at that moment, they were displaced; they were not expelled, whereas the people from Trnovo were expelled, through the use of force, physical force. Perhaps I was clearer now rather than when this paragraph was recorded. I did not realise that each and every word was that important, but I've tried to clarify it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then understand you well that you say that the population who lived in the town that were displaced, that it may have been under the circumstances around the town but not as a direct result of force exercised upon them? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: 1.000 to 1.500 inhabitants who had to leave Trnovo on that day and the following day were the population that was expelled. The others -- well, relatively speaking. Now, whether it was 900 people or 1.100 people, I really don't know exactly. But there were people who temporarily came to Trnovo and were put up there and they were expelled from Trnovo the following day too. So today they were displaced persons. We took care of them. They came from somewhere, but I cannot say whether they came from Foca because they were expelled by force or whether they became displaced persons out of fear. That's the distinction I'm making. So perhaps at first they were displaced and then they became expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say you do not know exactly whether any force was used when they left Foca, but once they had temporarily settled in Trnovo, they then left as a result of force? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the last time the word "displaced" is used, you intended to say "expelled"?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then my next question is about crisis staffs. You were asked about Muslim crisis staffs, and you said: Well, I did not know exactly how the different nationalities or ethnicities responded to what happened. At least you have got no knowledge of your own. But just as you told us about what you heard about SDS crisis staffs to be established, could you also tell us what you heard about similar activities from other groups, Bosniaks, as far as crisis staffs are concerned.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I think that the political parties at that time reacted -- well, each and every one of them in their own way. I wish to note that the SDA also established some bodies that they deemed necessary in order to defend themselves from certain things, and also to create conditions for their own work. However, in the work of the municipal authorities, this was not present. I cannot say for the SDS what their staff was like. I cannot say what the SDA staff was like. But also, I cannot assert that there weren't any such bodies in the SDA. I think that at that time, each and every political party reacted in a similar way to all of this, except that I know that the SDA did not have physical force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that last line, no physical force? That they had no weapons or no ...

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: At any rate, they did not have the weapons and the force that the other side had and that was manifested at checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "they did not have the weapons and the force," what do you mean exactly by "force"?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I'm measuring the activity of both political parties and I'm trying to make a distinction there. So even though they had some staffs, or crisis staffs, they could not have military formations, those that could directly threaten the population on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could they establish checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: They could, of course, but they could not have armed forces there as the SDS did. The police force, the regular police force of the public security station in Trnovo, remained within the system. So they did their job to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that you learned about the establishment of SDS crisis staffs in -- as you said, in Trnovo as well. What did you exactly know about what happened outside Trnovo? Because you said "in Trnovo as well," which suggests that you have some knowledge of what happened elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I think, or rather, facts indicate that Trnovo was one of the last municipalities to be engulfed by the war, out of the ten municipalities that made up the town of Sarajevo. In my opinion, that was one of the most peaceful municipalities for the longest period of time. I knew about other municipalities as well, since we were part of the city of Sarajevo. We often had meetings within the city assembly. The municipality of Pale had already carried out its separation from the city. It was one of the ten municipalities that was no longer part of the city, not because some kind of procedure had been carried through but because they had simply seceded. So perhaps I used the word "and" because of the knowledge I had myself and because of what I heard from other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vatric. Is there any need to ask further questions to the witness based on the questions put by the Bench? Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, there are, as a result of Your Honour's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you'll recall, Mr. Vatric, prior to my cross-examining you that His Honour asked you -- His Honour, the Presiding Judge, asked you -- when I asked you why you used the word that Muslims were expelled, you explained that they had to leave by force. Could you explain a little bit more what you mean by that, how this actually took place, what force was exercised, how precisely that went on. And your answer was that: "Well, the force came from artillery weapons. The town was shelled." And then you go on to say: "The unprotected civilian population in Trnovo was shelled, and this went on incessantly." And then: "That's why my colleague Mr. Durmo told me when he got out of Trnovo, this was the physical attack against Trnovo and there was no other way of protecting the population but getting them out to the neighbouring villages. That's what they did. They left during the night. They went from one house to the other, depending on who managed to do that. So it was direct force that was used coming from artillery weapons." So just to paraphrase what you gave in relation to that answer as your explanation of expelling and leaving by force, the situation is, what you're saying, is as a result of the shelling that was occurring, people were fleeing; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes. People left.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course, in relation to the evidence that you've given in relation to the -- through that paragraph 20, 2.500 people, of course, I take it you did not speak directly to all 2.500 people that we're dealing with here; correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Of course I did not speak to all 2.500 people, but I could not give you the exact number of people I spoke to. I did speak to a great many people, though, because I provided accommodation for them from the villages of Trnovo all the way down to Split. So I had ample knowledge from them as to why they had left, and that is a fact. Can I just ask you something else? You read something out to me a few minutes ago and you said something like "taking people out"? I can't remember the exact word you used. But Ekrem Durmo, when he was speaking, there was a particular word that was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: We can just check that on the transcript. We'll just do that now. "And there was no other way of protecting the population but getting them out to the neighbouring villages. That's what they did. They left during the night." That's the bit I quoted to you. That was part of your answer to His Honour the Presiding Judge. Is that the bit you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's the part I'm referring to. I'm not sure about this word "taking them out." Not the population. I wasn't referring to the population. I was referring to families. So in order to avoid any confusion there, it referred to families rather than the population. That's when I mentioned Ekrem Durmo.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Now, I think you indicated previously that you couldn't tell me exactly how many of these 2.500 people you actually spoke to. Could you give perhaps an approximation of the number of people you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: I don't know what a number would mean, but whichever number I give you is correct. Now, whether I'm going to tell you 100, 200, 300, whatever, but I am a person who took care of all these people. And whenever you meet people like that, you exchange a few words. So I think it would be a thankless thing for me to say 100, 200, 300, but I talked to all these people about what had directly happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vatric. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: OMER VATRIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Karagiannakis. Mr. Vatric, this, then, concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to answer all questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Vatric out of the courtroom. I wish you a safe trip home again, Mr. Vatric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did my best to carry out my obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber still has to deliver a decision in closed session, I would like to ask the parties whether there's anything else to be raised at this very moment. Because otherwise, we'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps one additional question to the Prosecution. Do we have already some information about exhibits, what is it, 200 up until 203?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The correspondence that was referred to by Defence counsel was directed to Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis is not here today. I will check with Mr. Hannis tomorrow and perhaps we can resolve this quickly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's, then, do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first give decision on the exhibits. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P322, witness statement dated 21 January 1998, and P322.1, B/C/S translation. P323, map of Sarajevo and surrounding municipalities, marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you objected against the language of the statement, especially in view of paragraph 20. Does that objection still stand? We -- as you may have noticed, it was at least at that moment the Chamber thought that it could be admitted, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please use --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honour. Of course, Your Honours made that preliminary indication in relation to admissibility on the basis of further evidence in chief, cross-examination. The area, of course, has been dealt with in evidence in chief, cross-examination, questions from the Chamber, and in those circumstances, it now seems futile to persist, of course, in that particular objection, because it's now been dealt with appropriately through viva voce questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then Exhibits 322 and 322.1 and 323, all proceeded by the letter P, are admitted in evidence. Then I'd like to turn into -- I said closed session, but perhaps, since it's just reading out a decision, that private session would do. Just looking to the parties, especially to you, Mr. Harmon. It's a decision about transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Private session is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Private session is fine. We'll then turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, tomorrow morning, 9.00, next witness will be available to be examined by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understood it was tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. It should be at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. As far as I understand, Madam Registrar, in Courtroom I? Yes, that will be in Courtroom I. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, a quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.
